sources.text:
US warns Iran of indefinite naval blockade as Strait of Hormuz deadlock continues
Mail This Article
The United States has threatened to maintain a naval blockade of Iran indefinitely and ratchet up economic pressure on Tehran even as ceasefire talks have floundered, global oil supply is dropping and regional tensions are rising.
According to Reuters, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told reporters on Thursday that the U.S. military had the capability to maintain a naval presence in the region to enforce its blockade of Iran, which he claimed had inflicted severe economic damage on the country.
"Indefinitely the United States Navy can maintain a blockade like that because we'll rotate ships in and out, as we have, and we'll continue to," Hegseth told reporters during a trip to Panama.
Meanwhile, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Thursday the United States planned to inflict more financial damage on Iran.
"Watch this space for more announcements coming next week because we are going to apply measures like have never been seen in the history of economic isolation on a country," he said in an interview on Newsmax's "Rob Schmitt Tonight" programme.
With a tentative June deal to end the war in tatters, Iran has sought to exert leverage on Washington in return by controlling the Strait of Hormuz. It has attacked some vessels trying to transit the strategic waterway, through which a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas traveled before the war began in February.
Two vessels from the state-owned Abu Dhabi National Oil Company were attacked transiting the strait on Thursday evening, UAE state news agency WAM reported. The United Arab Emirates government condemned it as an Iranian attack.
U.S. President Donald Trump is under pressure at home to end a war that is deeply unpopular, with high fuel prices dragging down his approval ratings and potentially eroding his party's control of Congress in midterm elections in November.
Trump has repeatedly asserted that the U.S. has "total control" over the strait, prompting Iranian denials. Tehran has said it will not allow the waterway to reopen until its conditions are met. These include removing economic sanctions and releasing frozen Iranian assets.
Shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz fell to eight vessels on Tuesday, compared with a 10-day average of about 12 vessels, and 130 to 140 ships before the war.
The U.S. lifted its blockade of Iran's shipping and ports for a month in mid-June but has since reimposed it, cutting off Tehran's primary source of hard currency and compounding earlier losses from wartime strikes on its energy infrastructure.
Washington previously said it would lift the Iranian blockade once Iran and Oman, which sit on either side of the strait, reach an agreement to restore commercial shipping.
Shrinking oil supply
Trump has also repeatedly threatened to escalate military strikes and "hit Iran hard", although he has thus far resisted deploying ground troops or seizing strategic islands and bombing desalination plants. Earlier this week, Trump suggested he would rely on economic means, rather than military action.
The U.S. has tightened economic sanctions against Iran and other individuals and entities that it says are helping it procure weapons, but the pressure campaign has failed to bring Tehran back to the negotiating table.
Stress is also mounting on the global economy. The International Energy Agency on Wednesday forecast that global oil supply would fall by 4.3 million barrels per day, or around 4%, this year. Just a month ago, the agency had forecast a drop of 3.7 million barrels per day.
Reports that Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis had targeted a Saudi Aramco refinery with drones also have unsettled the market, renewing concerns about a widening regional war.
Global economists have forecast a sharp drop in global growth as a result of the war, and potentially a swing into recession in some areas, warning that the impact will grow if the war is not ended soon.
Hegseth declined to comment on a question about whether, in retrospect, it was a mistake to declare a ceasefire in April, a move that ended high-tempo bombing of Iran in exchange for peace negotiations that have failed to resolve the conflict.
"I'm never going to comment on that. We're doing exactly what we need to, to ensure that Iran never has a nuclear weapon," Hegseth said.

sources.news_title: Oil Rebounds as Hegseth Vows Indefinite Iran Blockade
sources.text:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Thursday that the United States can maintain its naval blockade of Iranian ports indefinitely, framing the standoff over the Strait of Hormuz as a war of attrition the U.S. military is structurally positioned to win regardless of how long Tehran holds out. "Indefinitely the United States Navy can maintain a blockade like that because we'll rotate ships in and out, as we have, and we'll continue to," Hegseth told reporters in Panama City, where he had just addressed sailors aboard the guided-missile destroyer USS Gridley during a stop tied to regional security engagements. His remarks came a day after President Trump declared on Truth Social that "the U.S.A. has total control over the Strait of Hormuz," adding, "I think we will keep it," and describing the blockade as being called by "everyone" a "wall of steel."
Hegseth's comments landed hours after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent previewed a fresh round of economic measures against Tehran in unusually stark terms. "Watch this space for more announcements coming next week because we are going to apply measures like have never been seen in the history of economic isolation on a country," Bessent said, describing a strategy combining escalated financial pressure with the continued naval blockade. "It will be a combination of economic isolation like the world has never seen before, and the continued blockade in the Strait of Hormuz that will keep anything from going in or out of the Iranian ports," he said, adding that he expects the conflict's "temporary spike in energy prices" to eventually subside. Bessent did not detail what the new measures would target. Hegseth also pushed back on separate reporting about strained conditions for sailors deployed aboard the carrier USS Abraham Lincoln, calling the accounts "completely misrepresented" and saying every ship, crew and captain receives full support even though some deployments run longer than others.
The standoff traces back to February 28, when U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iranian military and government targets, including the killing of then-Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, triggered a war that has run for more than five months. Iran responded by effectively closing the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas had passed before the conflict. A June 17 memorandum of understanding between Washington and Tehran opened a 60-day window of toll-free passage for commercial vessels, but renewed Iranian attacks on shipping in late June and again in early July prompted U.S. airstrikes and led Trump to declare the memorandum no longer in force. The window created by that agreement is set to lapse around August 17, and no talks are currently underway to extend it.
The dual statements from two of the administration's most senior national security officials come as Iran has offered its clearest public signal yet that it is prepared to treat the standoff as a long-term war of attrition rather than a crisis to be resolved on a deadline. A top adviser to the commander of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, identified as Naqdi, said in an interview broadcast Wednesday that Tehran could "prolong" the war until Trump leaves office. "We have to attain deterrence so that the enemy never dares to attack us," he said. "One way is to prolong this war until we get to the next term of the presidency and cause attrition, so that if anyone else wants to attack Iran, they will know there is a cost." He argued Washington had shown "confusion and bewilderment" throughout the conflict, pointing to shifting American objectives that ranged from regime change to control of Kharg Island, and said Iran already considered itself victorious in having prevented both outcomes.
Iran's military leadership reinforced that defiance Thursday. Hossein Taeb, commander of Iran's Basij paramilitary force, asserted that the Strait of Hormuz remains "under Iran's control and management," directly contradicting Trump's claim of U.S. control. Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority, the body Tehran created in May to oversee shipping through the waterway, separately rejected the U.S. position in a social media post: "Claims and repeated posts by U.S. officials that the Strait of Hormuz is no longer blocked do not change the reality." Tehran has said the strait will not reopen until its conditions are met, chiefly the removal of economic sanctions and the release of frozen Iranian assets. U.S. Central Command has said it has redirected 59 commercial vessels attempting to enter or exit Iranian ports since reimposing the blockade on July 13, while maintaining its tally of three vessels disabled and two boarded.
Shipping data illustrate how far the waterway remains from normal operations regardless of who claims to control it. Vessel transits fell to a one-week low of eight on Wednesday, down from a five-day average of around 13 earlier in the week and roughly 94% below the daily average of 130 ships that transited Hormuz before the war began. The broader Gulf conflict has grown deadlier in parallel: six people aboard a vessel in the Red Sea were killed by Iran-backed Houthi rebels, Yemen's coast guard said Tuesday, adding to marine insurers' estimate that the conflict has generated $1.5 billion to $2 billion in claims from roughly 70 vessel casualties since late February. Earlier this week, a U.S. Navy MH-60 helicopter fired two Hellfire missiles into the engine room of a Panama-flagged ship after it ignored warnings from U.S. forces, according to the military.
Iran's newly installed security chief has hardened his own conditions for reopening the strait. Mohsen Rezaei, appointed over the weekend as secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, told China's ambassador to Tehran, Cong Peiwu, that Washington must end its military campaign and release Iranian funds frozen abroad before the strait can fully reopen. "As long as the U.S. does not change its behaviour and accept Iran's conditions, the Strait of Hormuz will not be reopened," Rezaei said, adding on social media that he was also insisting on an end to the U.S. naval blockade and a region-wide ceasefire extending to Gaza and Lebanon — conditions that go beyond what he had stated earlier in the week. Tehran has separately pressed a new grievance tied to environmental damage from the standoff, demanding compensation for oil pollution that has spread along more than a kilometer of coastline on Qeshm Island and into nearby mangrove forests, with officials still investigating the source.
Diplomatic efforts have continued at the margins without visible traction. Pakistan's Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi visited Tehran this week aiming to persuade Iran to resume negotiations with Washington under the expiring interim agreement, while Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesperson Majed al-Ansari said he had heard "positive messages" from both Tehran and Muscat regarding a possible reopening. Iran's parliament has continued moving in parallel to formalize its unilateral control over the strait; a bill approved by the National Security and Foreign Policy Commission — which would bar U.S.- and Israel-linked vessels from transiting and impose fines of up to 20% of cargo value on violators — is still awaiting a full floor vote, Guardian Council review and presidential signature.
Oil markets reversed direction Friday after two straight sessions of declines. Brent crude traded near $88 a barrel and U.S. West Texas Intermediate climbed above $82, gains that came despite softer demand forecasts and a sizable increase in U.S. crude inventories — pressures that would typically weigh on prices. Traders pointed to renewed Hormuz tensions alongside a separate disruption at Russia's Ust-Luga oil export hub following a Ukrainian drone attack, adding another supply concern layered atop the Gulf standoff. The International Energy Agency has said the global oil market faces a shortfall of about 1.8 million barrels a day this quarter, and does not expect Middle East oil production to return to near pre-conflict levels until early 2027 — a timeline that would place any recovery well beyond the current standoff's August 17 deadline no matter how the coming days unfold.
Whether Washington's twin threats of expanded economic isolation and indefinite naval pressure produce any movement from Tehran before that deadline passes remains an open question. Bessent's promised measures are still undisclosed, and Hegseth has signaled no change in U.S. military posture. For now, both sides continue trading escalatory declarations — an American war secretary vowing infinite patience, an Iranian paramilitary commander insisting on sovereign control — while the strait itself stays effectively closed to commercial traffic no matter which government claims to hold it.

sources.news_title: ‘Economic Fury’: Treasury Secretary Bessent Says U.S. to Hit Iran with Measures ‘Never Seen in History’
sources.text:
President Donald Trump is preparing to dramatically escalate his “Economic Fury” campaign against Iran, with new measures coming next week, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned Thursday.
He added the move has “never been seen in the history of economic isolation” while coupled with a U.S. naval blockade aimed at preventing anything from moving in or out of Iranian ports.
“Watch this space for more announcements coming next week,” Bessent said Thursday night on Newsmax’s Rob Schmitt Tonight. “We are going to apply measures like have never been seen in the history of economic isolation on a country.”
Bessent described the coming measures as the latest escalation of a pressure campaign Trump restored after returning to office and has steadily intensified against the Iranian regime.
“A year ago, March of ’25, the president gave me the order to apply maximum pressure to the Iranian regime, and Treasury did,” Bessent said.
Since then, he said, Treasury has gone after Iranian “bank accounts, crypto wallets, assets around the world,” while cutting off financial flows to regime leaders and the government itself.
Bessent pointed to the collapse of a major Iranian bank late last year to illustrate the impact Treasury was already having before the current conflict began, saying the failure forced Iran’s central bank to print money and fueled a surge in inflation as the country’s economy deteriorated.
The military phase that began in February marked another turn. After weeks of U.S. strikes under Operation Epic Fury, Bessent said the administration shifted toward a new phase centered on tightening the financial pressure on Tehran.
“We went from Epic Fury to Economic Fury,” he said.
Trump has now ordered Treasury to raise that pressure again.
“At the president’s orders, we have raised the level even again,” Bessent said.
Bessent described the strategy as a “one-two punch” combining economic isolation with the continuing U.S. blockade of Iranian ports.
“It will be a combination of economic isolation like the world has never seen before and the continued blockade in the Strait of Hormuz that will keep anything from going in or out of the Iranian ports,” he said.
His remarks capped a day in which senior Trump administration officials publicly laid out different elements of the same strategy: tighten the economic vise, sustain maritime pressure for as long as necessary, restore more stable energy flows through the Gulf, and preserve overwhelming military force if Tehran chooses to escalate.
Vice President JD Vance described the broader approach Thursday as the deliberate use of diplomatic, economic, and military power toward two overriding goals: preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon and returning Hormuz to conditions that stabilize energy prices.
“The thing I can say with confidence is I think this ends with the United States in a stronger position, with Iran not having a nuclear weapon, and with the Strait of Hormuz returned to a place where oil and gas prices are stable for the American people,” Vance said during an interview with Fox News host Will Cain.
Asked about the apparent “seesaw” between diplomacy, military threats, and economic pressure, Vance said the shifts instead reflect the range of options available to Trump.
“You’re seeing a president of the United States at the height of his authority with a lot of tools — diplomatic, military, and economic,” Vance said.
The administration, he added, is using those tools “very selectively, very strategically” to produce the outcome Trump is seeking.
War Secretary Pete Hegseth made the maritime component equally explicit earlier Thursday, saying the Navy can sustain the blockade for as long as necessary and directly rejecting any calculation in Tehran that it can simply wait Washington out.
“We can hold the blockade as long as we need to. Indefinitely,” Hegseth told reporters in Panama.
The Navy can maintain that pressure by rotating ships through the region, Hegseth said, before invoking the same phrase Trump has used to describe the blockade.
“No other nation on Earth, no other Navy on Earth, can have a ‘wall of steel’ like the U.S. Navy — and then the willingness to use it as we have,” he said.
Hegseth then made the intended message to Tehran unmistakable.
“Iran knows it can’t get in and out on this blockade,” he said. “They know there’s no timeline on it either.”
Trump has repeatedly driven home the same point, declaring Wednesday that Washington has “total control” of Hormuz and indicating that he intends to maintain it.
“The U.S.A. has total control over the Strait of Hormuz. I THINK WE WILL KEEP IT!” Trump wrote on Truth Social.
“Our Naval Blockade is being called, by everyone, ‘A WALL OF STEEL,’ and there is nothing Iran can do about it,” he added.
The administration is also arguing that Iran’s ability to use Hormuz as economic leverage is shrinking even as Washington becomes more capable of moving Gulf energy supplies through and around the waterway.
Energy Secretary Chris Wright said Thursday that Tehran remains capable of disrupting regional commerce but is pursuing what he called a “losing strategy.”
“Iran is attempting to hold the world economy hostage and to terrorize their neighbors,” Wright told Fox News’ Bret Baier.
He said sustained pressure would ultimately “lead to the collapse of this regime in Iran as their economy gets strangled.”
Wright argued that the balance is gradually shifting against Tehran.
“Their ability to cause difficulties are declining. Our ability to escort and bring products out of that region is growing,” he said. “They have sort of one card, and it’s shrinking in size.”
Wright said U.S. government data show roughly eight to nine million barrels of oil per day are currently moving through Hormuz — significantly more than some commercial vessel-tracking estimates have indicated.
He explained that many vessels are moving under U.S. military escort with their Automatic Identification System (AIS) transponders switched off, meaning commercial tracking services cannot reliably see every transit.
“We’re talking and coordinating with every ship,” Wright said, adding that the government receives daily information on vessels moving through the strait and what they are carrying.
Combined with roughly six million barrels per day being moved through alternative pipelines, Wright estimated that approximately 14 million to 15 million barrels are now leaving the Arabian Gulf region each day, compared with roughly 20 million before the conflict.
Tehran, however, is signaling that it may answer the mounting American pressure by escalating rather than yielding.
Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser to Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, said Thursday that Khamenei’s “definitive strategy” would be to move Iran onto the offensive if Washington refuses Tehran’s sweeping conditions.
“The Supreme Leader’s definitive strategy of shifting the war to an offensive posture if Iran’s conditions are not met will undoubtedly transform the balance of power in the world,” Mokhber wrote on X.
Iran’s Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters likewise rejected Washington’s claims of control over Hormuz as “lies and falsehoods,” insisting that the strait remains under Tehran’s “complete management and control.”
The Iranian command declared that “no commercial or oil tanker can transit this strait safely without the authorization and supervision of Iran’s powerful armed forces.”
Trump has repeatedly warned Tehran about the consequences of trying to challenge Washington’s position.
“We have total control over the Hormuz Strait right now,” Trump said earlier this week. “They don’t have control. We have total control. We own it.”
He then made clear what he believes would follow another Iranian escalation.
“At some point, maybe they’ll do something, and then they get blown away.”
The confrontation is increasingly becoming a contest between two competing strategies: Washington is betting that Tehran cannot economically withstand an open-ended blockade combined with escalating financial isolation, while Iran is threatening to widen the conflict if the United States refuses its demands.
Bessent, meanwhile, made clear Thursday that Washington’s economic campaign is moving in only one direction.
“We went from Epic Fury to Economic Fury,” he said. “And at the president’s orders, we have raised the level even again.”

sources.text:
The United States said Thursday it could sustain a naval blockade of Iran indefinitely while stepping up economic pressure on Tehran as ceasefire talks stall, global oil supplies tighten and tensions across the region escalate.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the U.S. military has the capacity to sustain a naval presence in the region to enforce the blockade, which has already inflicted severe economic damage on Iran.
“The United States Navy can maintain a blockade like that indefinitely because we’ll rotate ships in and out, as we have, and we’ll continue to,” Hegseth told reporters during a trip to Panama.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent separately said Thursday that Washington planned to further increase financial pressure on Iran as part of its broader effort to weaken Tehran’s economy.
“Watch this space for more announcements coming next week because we are going to apply measures like have never been seen in the history of economic isolation on a country,” he said in an interview on Newsmax’s “Rob Schmitt Tonight” program.
With a tentative June deal to end the war in tatters, Iran has sought to exert leverage on Washington by controlling the Strait of Hormuz.
It has attacked some vessels attempting to transit the strategic waterway, through which one-fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas traveled before the war began in February.
Two vessels operated by state-owned Abu Dhabi National Oil Co. were attacked while transiting the strait Thursday evening, the UAE state news agency WAM reported. The United Arab Emirates government condemned the incident as an Iranian attack.
U.S. President Donald Trump is under pressure at home to end a war that is deeply unpopular, with high fuel prices weighing on his approval ratings and potentially eroding his party’s control of Congress in November’s midterm elections.
Trump has repeatedly asserted that the U.S. has “total control” over the strait, prompting Iranian denials. Tehran has said it will not allow the waterway to reopen until its conditions are met, including the removal of economic sanctions and the release of frozen Iranian assets.
Shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz fell to eight vessels Tuesday, compared with a 10-day average of about 12 vessels and 130 to 140 ships before the war.
The U.S. lifted its blockade of Iran’s shipping and ports for a month in mid-June but has since reimposed it, cutting off Tehran’s primary source of hard currency and compounding earlier losses from wartime strikes on its energy infrastructure.
Washington previously said it would lift the blockade once Iran and Oman, which sit on either side of the strait, reach an agreement to restore commercial shipping.
Trump has also repeatedly threatened to escalate military strikes and “hit Iran hard,” although he has so far resisted deploying ground troops, seizing strategic islands or bombing desalination plants. Earlier this week, Trump suggested he would rely on economic means rather than military action.
The U.S. has tightened economic sanctions against Iran and other individuals and entities that it says are helping Tehran procure weapons, but the pressure campaign has failed to bring Tehran back to the negotiating table.
Stress is mounting on the global economy. The International Energy Agency on Wednesday forecast that global oil supply would fall by 4.3 million barrels per day, or about 4%, this year.
Just a month ago, the agency had forecast a decline of 3.7 million barrels per day.
Oil prices settled more than 2% lower Thursday after a week of gains as investors focused on signs of weaker global demand and a sharp increase in U.S. crude inventories.
But reports that Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis had targeted a Saudi Aramco refinery with drones unsettled the market, renewing concerns about a widening regional war.
Global economists have forecast a sharp drop in global growth as a result of the war and potentially a swing into recession in some areas, warning that the impact will grow if the war is not ended soon.
Hegseth declined to comment when asked whether, in retrospect, it was a mistake to declare a ceasefire in April, a move that ended high-tempo bombing of Iran in exchange for peace negotiations that have failed to resolve the conflict.
“I’m never going to comment on that. We’re doing exactly what we need to, to ensure that Iran never has a nuclear weapon,” Hegseth said.

sources.news_title: US to roll out ‘economic isolation’ plan for Iran next week
sources.text:
The US will soon announce what it bills as unprecedented economic measures against Iran, treasury secretary Scott Bessent said, intensifying the Trump administration’s effort to force Tehran’s capitulation through financial pressure.
“Watch this space for more announcements coming next week because we are going to apply measures like have never been seen in the history of economic isolation on a country,” Bessent said Thursday in an interview with Newsmax.
Bessent said the move would be part of a “one-two punch” that included the continued blockade of Iran’s ports.
Iran’s economy has already taken a significant hit from the war, with much of its industrial capacity destroyed and crude exports severely curtailed by the US blockade. But the country has weathered waves of sanctions, which have failed to force Tehran to bend on its nuclear program or relinquish control over the Strait of Hormuz.
READ MORE
President Donald Trump in recent days has renewed his administration’s push for economic pressure on Iran as the US faces a shortfall of necessary munitions and appears wary of expanding its military campaign.
Trump told Axios over the weekend that he was “low-keying it” with Iran. “We are just watching Iran with its huge inflation and the fact they have no money,” he said.
Iran, for its part, has reorganised its military to be more aggressive abroad as talks on ending the war with the US remain in stalemate, a sign that Tehran is preparing for a protracted era of regional conflict.
There is little sign of a breakthrough between Iran and the US over the Strait of Hormuz. Both sides claim control of the waterway, through which a fifth of the world’s oil and gas is shipped, and are demanding concessions that are unlikely to be met.
Oil held losses, with Brent trading near $87 a barrel after falling 2.2 per cent in the previous session.
Over the weekend, Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said a pact with Oman to establish a shipping route through the strait was “very close,” without providing details.
The two sides have not yet announced an agreement. – Bloomberg

sources.news_title: Iran war; no genuinely safe shipping route in area
sources.text:
Here's the latest
• Iran war: US President Donald Trump said Friday he would “never apologize” for taking military action against Iran. “I did the right thing,” he said, arguing higher gas prices have been worth it in pursuit of preventing Iran from having a nuclear weapon.
• Strait of Hormuz: Trump said he plans to declare the waterway a US territory after “we finish defeating Iran.” Declaring the strait a US territory would necessitate deploying troops in the area indefinitely — at the least — though Trump previously vowed to keep the war brief.
• US carrier concerns: A second sailor deployed with the USS Abraham Lincoln strike group went overboard last spring, according to US officials. The report comes as the US sends another carrier group to the Middle East to replace the Lincoln, a US official told CNN, adding that the swap was planned.
• In depth: View our interactive on how Strait of Hormuz traffic has adapted to each phase of the Middle East conflict.
"I'll never apologize," Trump says about war that's resulted in higher gas prices
President Donald Trump said he would “never apologize” for taking military action against Iran, arguing that higher gas prices have been worth it in his pursuit of preventing Iran from having a nuclear weapon.
“For you to pay a tiny little bit more for your gasoline, just remember you’re doing it so that a very evil country cannot have — a country, really, it’s the number one state sponsor of terror in the world — we don’t want to have them have a nuclear weapon. So remember that when you have to pay a little bit more,” Trump said at an event in Nassau County, New York, on Friday.
He minimized the financial toll of the war on Americans, saying his decision to strike Iran was the “right” one.
“You’re at $4. It’s okay. I mean, it’s — I’m not, I’m not, I’ll never apologize. I did the right thing,” he said.
Just a couple hours earlier, outgoing White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said that the goals of keeping gas prices low and ensuring Iran never has a nuclear weapon are equally important to the president, an apparent shift in messaging from the administration’s initial focus on the nuclear issue.
The AAA national average for a gallon of regular is $4.07 Friday, up from $3.85 a month ago and $3.16 a year ago.
Throughout the war, Trump has argued higher gas prices are a small price to pay to ensure Iran doesn’t have a nuclear weapon. But in a recent CNN poll, 74% of Americans said the war was not worth the toll taken in American lives and the financial burden on the US government.
Houthi ballistic missile attack hits Yemen's strategic Red Sea port of Mokha
The Houthis launched six ballistic missiles at Yemen’s port of Mokha, on the Red Sea, according to Colonel Majid Abdullah al-Nuzaili, military spokesperson for Yemen’s Internationally Recognized Government.
“The Houthis’ targeting of ports amounts to besieging and starving the free Yemeni people,” al-Nuzaili said.
Houthi Armed Forces spokesperson Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said the attacks targeted “Saudi military concentrations and weapons, as well as war boats belonging to its proxies and mercenaries” in Mokha.
Saudi Arabia has not yet commented.
The kingdom has faced increasing attacks from the Houthis, who also declared a blockade on the al-Mandeb Strait in the Red Sea on July 20.
Trump says he plans to declare the Strait of Hormuz a US territory
President Donald Trump said Friday that he plans to declare the Strait of Hormuz a US territory after “we finish defeating Iran.”
He said that would happen “pretty soon.” Declaring the international waterway a US territory would necessitate deploying troops in the area indefinitely, at the least, though Trump had previously vowed to keep the war in Iran brief.
“We have the blockade,” Trump told a rally crowd in Nassau County. “No ships get through unless we want them to.”
Nearly half a year into the US-Iran war, global oil stockpiles are rapidly diminishing as traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains effectively stalled and the two powers at the center of the hostilities argue about who controls the critical waterway.
Iran says it won’t reopen the strait fully until the United States meets its conditions.
Trump, though, has repeatedly insisted that the strait — through which oil flows from countries like Saudi Arabia and Iraq to the rest of the world — is under US control.
“They don’t have control. We have total control. We own it, and at some point, maybe they’ll do something, and then they get blown away,” Trump told reporters on Wednesday. “Right now, we’re in a very good position.”
White House shifts message on Iran: Low gas prices equally important to nuclear goals
White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said the goal of keeping gas prices low and ensuring Iran never has a nuclear weapon are of equal importance to President Donald Trump — a shift from the administration’s frequent insistence that nothing is more important than blunting Iran’s nuclear capabilities.
“I think both goals are equally as important to the president: We want to keep gas prices low but also ensuring Iran can never get a nuclear weapon. Something he will see through no matter what,” Leavitt told reporters traveling on Air Force One.
Vice President JD Vance told Fox News on Thursday that “goal number one” is keeping gas and oil prices “cheap” for Americans, while deeming “goal number two” ensuring “that Iran never gets a nuclear weapon.”
When previously asked if he thinks about Americans’ financial situation when negotiating with Iran, Trump said in May, “Not even a little bit.”
“The only thing that matters when I’m talking about Iran [is] they can’t have a nuclear weapon,” he said at the time. “I don’t think about Americans’ financial situation. I don’t think about anybody. I think about one thing: We cannot let Iran have a nuclear weapon. That’s all.”
Sailor went overboard off a separate ship in the USS Lincoln strike group this spring
A second sailor deployed to the Middle East as part of the USS Abraham Lincoln strike group went overboard last spring, according to a sailor currently serving on the Lincoln and two US officials.
The crew member who went overboard was serving on the USS Frank E. Petersen Jr., a destroyer that is part of the Lincoln strike group, one of the officials said, adding that the incident occurred on April 12.
The sailor was rescued and then brought onto the Lincoln for medical treatment before being flown off of the carrier for further care, according to the Lincoln sailor and one of the officials.
It was not immediately clear if the sailor had jumped into the water, or had fallen in.
The man overboard incident off of the Petersen is the first reported on any of the other ships in the Lincoln strike group.
CNN was first to report about a sailor who officials said jumped into the water off of the Lincoln in early August during a mental health incident.
The Lincoln crew member who described the rescue of the sailor from the Petersen said that he also witnessed the August incident, saying he “saw the sailor run and jump off with my own eyes.” He described the sailor in the water as removing his life vest and boots while treading water.
Sailors do fall into the water accidentally on occasion, and ships on deployments also regularly face issues with suicidal ideation and attempts. All ships practice man overboard drills to respond to either scenario.
A Navy official downplayed reports about a growing mental health crisis on board the ship, saying in a statement:
“We have not observed an increase in suicidal ideations or attempts aboard the ship. We take every service member’s well-being seriously and have religious, medical and mental health professionals available to assess and address concerns as they arise.”
CNN has reached out to the Navy and US Central Command about the incident with the sailor jumping off the strike group ship but did not receive a response before publication.
No genuinely safe route for shipping in region, says maritime intelligence group
Commercial shipping attempting to navigate in and around the Persian Gulf faces the dual threats of violence in the Strait of Hormuz and Houthi attacks in the Bab al-Mandeb, meaning that there is “currently no genuinely ‘safe’ side of the Arabian Peninsula,” said maritime intelligence group Marisks in their latest intelligence update.
The maritime security situation in the region “has entered a more dangerous phase,” Marisks said. That is due to the “simultaneous emergence” of the US enforcing its blockade of Iranian ports, as well as “targeted attacks at both the Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb,” which are the two key trade routes out of the energy-rich Gulf countries.
“The two chokepoints can no longer be assessed independently,” the report said. “Pressure at Hormuz is transferring traffic and strategic importance toward Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea outlets, while Houthi pressure against Saudi interests simultaneously threatens that alternative.”
It pointed to several incidents this week, which represent an increased threat level – a fatal strike on a commercial vessel sailing through the Bab al-Mandeb strait; the US military disabling a cargo vessel sailing toward an Iranian port by firing two missiles into its engine room; and a UAE oil company accusing Iran of attacking several of its vessels recently.
Attacks on vessels using the Omani route shows that “Iran appears capable of projecting anti-ship effects across the southern transit area,” Marisks said.
The shipping industry has adapted to these threats, Marisks noted. In the three weeks since the US reimposed its blockade of Iranian ports, more than half of all tankers crossing the Strait of Hormuz turned off their transponders to avoid detection while more very large crude carriers have been used than at any point this year, Marisks said.
“This does not indicate normalisation,” the group said. “It indicates commercial adaptation to prolonged disruption.”
Vessel sustains “minor damage” after being hit by drone in Strait of Hormuz, UKMTO says
A vessel was struck by a drone yesterday while travelling through the Strait of Hormuz, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) center, which monitors maritime security.
The vessel had sustained “minor damages,” and all crew members were reported safe with no environmental damages reported. The agency did not identify the vessel or say who launched the drone.
Since Iran’s blockade of the strait, a limited number of vessels have been able to safely transit the waterway. Thirteen vessels passed through yesterday, whereas an estimated 120 vessels would pass through the waterway daily before the US-Iran war, according to maritime intelligence firm Kpler.
The US military has also imposed a blockade on ships sailing to and from Iranian ports, seeking to economically pressure Tehran into reopening the trade artery.
Since the war began, UKMTO has received more than 50 reports of incidents involving damages to vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, the Persian Gulf or the Gulf of Oman.
CNN’s Issy Roland contributed to this report.
Just 13 vessels crossed Strait of Hormuz on Thursday, says maritime intelligence firm
Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz is still incredibly limited with only 13 vessels crossing the waterway on Thursday, according to maritime intelligence firm Kpler.
That marked a slight increase from nine vessels making the crossing on Wednesday but still does not reflect US President Donald Trump’s repeated insistence earlier this week that the strait is “open” and under American control.
Nine of the 13 vessels on Thursday followed the Iranian-approved route that the US has warned ships against taking. The other four switched off their tracking transponders to avoid detection so their route is unknown.
And the dangers faced by vessels attempting to navigate the crucial waterway was underlined Thursday night when the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC) said two of its ships had been attacked in the strait.
As the world burns through its oil stockpiles, the urgency of reopening the strait is becoming more pressing, the International Energy Agency warned Wednesday, even as oil prices have fallen.
CNN’s Mohammed Tawfeeq and Hanna Ziady contributed reporting.
A look at the risks and complications ships encounter in the Strait of Hormuz
Iran and Oman have long shared the waters in the Strait of Hormuz, and since 1968 vessels have traveled through a route established by the International Maritime Organization. In 1974, both countries signed an agreement at the United Nations defining the maritime boundaries in the strait.
Since the war began in February, Iran has exchanged strikes with US forces along the strait and is negotiating with Oman to rethink the long-established routes.
A look at the options ship crew have and the risks they face:
“Danger zone”: Early in the conflict, Iran designated the pre-war route a danger zone and said it had laid mines in the waterway. Ships have still been sailing through, but it is a dangerous option.
Omani route: This route was agreed upon by the International Maritime Organization, but has been rejected by Iran. Ships using this route have been attacked by Iran.
Iranian route: Iran says ships should only use its route and has set up the Persian Gulf Strait Authority (PGSA) to collect fees from vessels passing through the strait. The US has sanctioned the PGSA — meaning anyone who pays Iran to pass could potentially face future US sanctions.
Unknown route: Some ships are still taking a “dark” route to evade surveillance and attacks. This raises the risk of accidents or collisions and can void their insurance.
New risks have caused maritime insurance premiums to skyrocket. Maritime insurance to cross the strait is priced between 7.5% and 10% of a vessel’s value — up from 0.25% before the war.
See how traffic through the Strait of Hormuz is adapting to the war.
What to know about the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier
Reports of low morale and mental health concerns among sailors aboard the aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln have raised questions from Congress and families this week.
The aircraft carrier has been deployed for more than 250 days after being redirected to the Middle East to support US operations in the war with Iran. It has not made a port call in more than 200 days.

Keeping morale high on ships the size of US Navy aircraft carriers presents problems that smaller warships may not face, even in times of combat, experienced naval officers say.
Reports have surfaced this week of mental health concerns aboard the carrier USS Abraham Lincoln as its crew endures more than 200 days without a port call during operations against Iran.
A sailor was rescued after going overboard earlier this month off of the Lincoln, officials said. The sailor was not injured, and the Navy considered the incident a mental health episode, according to one official.
With more than 5,000 people aboard, keeping them all unified and focused as one team is difficult in a ship larger than some small towns, said Jennifer Parker, a former Royal Australian Navy officer and nonresident fellow at the Lowy Institute.
Parker served on Australian destroyers, with a crew of around 200, a size that enabled to commanding officer and executive officer to know the entire ship’s company personally, she said.
But top officers can’t have that kind of relationship with 5,000 sailors, she said.
“I think that would be a much harder leadership proposition on a carrier,” let alone a carrier in wartime conditions, Parker said.
Former US Navy Capt. Carl Schuster, who served three tours on the Lincoln’s sister ship, the USS Nimitz, in the late 1970s and 1980s, said life aboard can be isolating, especially for enlisted crew who work deep inside the 100,000-ton carriers.
“I was an officer, so my work was more mentally than physically focused, and I was out on bridge wings and flight deck several times a day,” Schuster told CNN.
Schuster said even in non-wartime conditions, mental health is a concern.
On each of his three deployments aboard the Nimitz, including two with at least 80 days straight at sea, at least two crew attempted suicide, he said.

And that doesn’t count other Navy demands on the carrier fleet, like exercises with allies or keeping a presence in the Indo-Pacific, Parker said.

PANAMA CITY — The United States on Thursday threatened to maintain a naval blockade of Iran indefinitely, ratcheting up economic pressure on Tehran as ceasefire talks have floundered, global oil supply is dropping and regional tensions are rising.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told reporters that the US military has the capability to maintain a naval presence in the region to enforce its blockade of Iran, which has inflicted severe economic damage on the country.
“Indefinitely the United States Navy can maintain a blockade like that because we’ll rotate ships in and out, as we have, and we’ll continue to,” Hegseth told reporters during a trip to Panama.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Washington plans to impose unprecedented economic measures on Iran, with further announcements expected next week.
"Watch this space for more announcements coming next week because we are going to apply measures like have never been seen in the history of economic isolation on a country," Bessent said in an interview with Newsmax's “Rob Schmitt Tonight” program on THursday.
Bessent said the measures would combine increased economic pressure on Tehran with restrictions related to the Strait of Hormuz.
"It will be a combination of economic isolation like the world has never seen before, and the continued blockade in the Strait of Hormuz that will keep anything from going in or out of the Iranian ports," he said.
With a tentative June deal to end the war in tatters, Iran has sought to exert leverage on Washington in return by controlling the Strait of Hormuz.
It has attacked some vessels trying to transit the strategic waterway, through which a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas traveled before the war began in February.
Two vessels from the state-owned Abu Dhabi National Oil Company were attacked transiting the strait on Thursday evening, UAE state news agency WAM reported.
In a statement, the UAE Foreign Ministry said no injuries were reported in the attack, which it said was a "flagrant violation" of UN Security Council Resolution 2817 on freedom of navigation.
The ministry accused Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) of "acts of piracy," saying the use of the Strait of Hormuz as a tool of "economic coercion or blackmail" poses a direct threat to the region and its peoples.
The UAE called on Iran to halt what it described as "unprovoked attacks" and fully commit to an immediate cessation of hostilities.
US President Donald Trump is under pressure at home to end a war that is deeply unpopular, with high fuel prices dragging down his approval ratings and potentially eroding his party’s control of Congress in midterm elections in November.
Trump has repeatedly asserted that the US has “total control” over the strait, prompting Iranian denials. Tehran has said it will not allow the waterway to reopen until its conditions are met. These include removing economic sanctions and releasing frozen Iranian assets.
Shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz fell to eight vessels on Tuesday, compared with a 10-day average of about 12 vessels, and 130 to 140 ships before the war.
The US lifted its blockade of Iran’s shipping and ports for a month in mid-June but has since reimposed it, cutting off Tehran’s primary source of hard currency and compounding earlier losses from wartime strikes on its energy infrastructure.
Washington previously said it would lift the Iranian blockade once Iran and Oman, which sit on either side of the strait, reach an agreement to restore commercial shipping.
Trump has also repeatedly threatened to escalate military strikes and “hit Iran hard,” although he has thus far resisted deploying ground troops or seizing strategic islands and bombing desalination plants. Earlier this week, Trump suggested he would rely on economic means, rather than military action.
The US has tightened economic sanctions against Iran and other individuals and entities that it says are helping it procure weapons, but the pressure campaign has failed to bring Tehran back to the negotiating table.
Stress is mounting on the global economy. The International Energy Agency on Wednesday forecast that global oil supply would fall by 4.3 million barrels per day, or around 4 percent, this year.
Just a month ago, the agency had forecast a drop of 3.7 million barrels per day.

Hegseth declined to comment on a question about whether, in retrospect, it was a mistake to declare a ceasefire in April, a move that ended high-tempo bombing of Iran in exchange for peace negotiations that have failed to resolve the conflict.
“I’m never going to comment on that. We’re doing exactly what we need to, to ensure that Iran never has a nuclear weapon,” Hegseth said.

US signals long-term Iran naval blockade as Hormuz tensions squeeze oil flows
The United States says it can keep its naval blockade of Iran in place for as long as needed. The standoff is deepening Strait of Hormuz risks and fresh worries over global energy supplies.
The United States has indicated it is prepared to maintain its naval blockade of Iran for an extended period, increasing economic pressure on Tehran as efforts to secure a lasting ceasefire remain stalled and concerns grow over tightening global energy supplies.
Speaking during a visit to Panama, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the US Navy could sustain the blockade indefinitely by rotating ships in and out of the region. His remarks underscored Washington's determination to keep pressure on Iran despite mounting concerns over the broader economic impact of the conflict.
"Indefinitely the United States Navy can maintain a blockade like that because we'll rotate ships in and out, as we have, and we'll continue to," Hegseth said.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the United States was preparing to intensify economic pressure on Iran, signalling that additional sanctions and financial measures could be announced in the coming days.
Speaking on Newsmax's Rob Schmitt Tonight, Bessent said Washington was planning unprecedented steps to further isolate Tehran economically.
"Watch this space for more announcements coming next week because we are going to apply measures like have never been seen in the history of economic isolation on a country," he said.
The blockade has become a central element of the US strategy against Iran, targeting the country's shipping and port operations and restricting a key source of foreign currency earnings. Washington briefly eased the restrictions for a month in June but later reimposed them after diplomatic efforts failed to produce a breakthrough.
The latest comments come amid renewed tensions in and around the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most important energy corridors. Before the conflict erupted in February, roughly one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade passed through the waterway.
Iran has repeatedly insisted that the strait will not be fully reopened until its conditions are met, including the removal of economic sanctions and the release of frozen Iranian assets. US President Donald Trump, meanwhile, has maintained that Washington retains control over security in the strategic passage.
Tensions escalated further on Thursday after two vessels operated by the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC) were reportedly attacked while transiting the Strait of Hormuz. The United Arab Emirates condemned the incident and blamed Iran, describing it as an attack on commercial shipping and freedom of navigation.
The security situation has contributed to a sharp decline in maritime traffic through the strait. Shipping volumes have fallen significantly from pre-war levels, highlighting the continuing disruption to global trade and energy flows.
The standoff is also adding to concerns about the global oil market. The International Energy Agency this week raised its estimate for the decline in global oil supply this year, warning that production losses are deepening as the conflict drags on. The agency now expects global supply to fall by 4.3 million barrels per day, compared with an earlier forecast of 3.7 million barrels per day.
Although oil prices fell on Thursday amid concerns over weakening demand and rising US crude inventories, markets remain sensitive to developments in the Middle East. Reports that Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement targeted a Saudi Aramco refinery with drones have fuelled fears of a broader regional escalation.
Economists have warned that a prolonged conflict and continued disruption to energy supplies could slow global growth and increase recession risks in several economies. With ceasefire negotiations showing little progress, uncertainty over the future of the Strait of Hormuz and global oil markets continues to weigh on investors and governments alike.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent declared on Thursday that Washington is preparing to execute economic actions against Tehran on a scale never previously attempted.
"Watch this space for more announcements coming next week because we are going to apply measures like have never been seen in the history of economic isolation on a country," Bessent told Newsmax in an interview.
"It will be a combination of economic isolation like the world has never seen before, and the continued blockade in the Strait of Hormuz that will keep anything from going in or out of the Iranian ports," he added.
Bessent's warnings follow statements made earlier Thursday on Fox News by US Vice President JD Vance, who defined America's primary goals in the ongoing standoff as guaranteeing global energy market stability and stopping Tehran from securing nuclear capabilities.
Outlining Washington's two main mandates, Vance stated, “It's ensuring that the Gulf countries continue to send oil and gas to the world economy so that we have energy price stability. That's obviously important for the American people. I know that oil is down today and it's way down from the highs in the early days of the conflict. That's goal number one, keep oil and gas cheap for Americans all over our country."
“And then obviously goal number two is [to] ensure that Iran never gets a nuclear weapon. I feel confident we're accomplishing both of those goals, but it's inherently an unpredictable thing because the Iranians themselves are unpredictable and they sometimes don't honor the commitments they've made to us," Vance concluded.
These comments align with recent declarations from President Donald Trump concerning the trajectory of the conflict.
Earlier in the week, when asked by a reporter whether a significant escalation remained an option - following prior warnings that ongoing diplomatic talks were Iran's final opportunity before "decapitation" - Trump answered, “You’ll find out."
When pressed further on whether a massive escalation was still under consideration, Trump stated, “Well, we certainly have that ability if we want to do that. You’ll find out."
The following day, speaking to reporters on the tarmac after traveling to Ohio, Trump underscored his deep skepticism of Iranian authorities while asserting firm US military control over vital sea routes.
"Iran is going fine, going just absolutely fine," Trump said, adding, “I'm the last person to trust Iran. They've lied to me constantly. We have total control over the Hormuz Strait right now. They don't have control. We have total control. We own it. And at some point, maybe they'll do something, and then they get blown away."

sources.text:
US President Donald Trump said he would "soon" declare the Strait of Hormuz part of US territory, claiming that Iran was being heavily defeated.
"After we finish defeating Iran, which is being very badly defeated - pretty soon I'll be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States," he said during a political rally at a police academy in New York state.
Mr Trump, together with Israel, launched a war against Iran on 28 February with the stated aims of ending the country's controversial nuclear programme and sparking a popular uprising.
However, Iran struck back by establishing de facto control over much of the Strait of Hormuz, a vital passageway for large amounts of global energy and other commodity shipping.
The United States remains locked in a stalemate with Iran over the strait, with Iran denying access to much of the civilian shipping and the US Navy mounting a blockade of Iranian ports.
"We have the blockade. No ships get through unless we want them to," Mr Trump told a cheering crowd of supporters.
It comes as transit through the vital waterway appeared to grind to a near standstill after two more ships were attacked there.
A senior Iranian source said that there had been no progress in talks to build on a June agreement to end the war.
As a ceasefire renewed then broke down, Iran has resumed attacks on ships it accuses of trying to transit the strait without its permission.
Two vessels from the state-owned Abu Dhabi National Oil Company were attacked transiting the strait yesterday evening, the United Arab Emirates state news agency WAM reported.
The UAE government blamed Iran, which made no immediate comment.
Nine vessels passed through the narrow waterway at the entrance to the Gulf yesterday, up from five on Wednesday but below the average of 12 for August, according to ship-tracking company Kpler.
There were no visible crossings by vessels seen early this morning, according to ship-tracking data.
Some ships may pass through undetected with their transponders off, but the figures are nowhere near the more than 130 ships that daily traversed the Strait of Hormuz before the war launched.
"Alongside the threat to energy infrastructure in the region, Iran's ability to restrict shipping through the strait is its main source of leverage in negotiations," said Torbjorn Solvedt, principal Middle East analyst with risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft.
US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth echoed Mr Trump's comments, telling reporters the US military has the capability to maintain a naval presence in the region to enforce its retaliatory blockade of Iran, which has inflicted severe economic damage on the country.
"Indefinitely the United States Navy can maintain a blockade like that because we'll rotate ships in and out, as we have, and we'll continue to," Mr Hegseth told reporters during a trip to Panama.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the United States planned to inflict more financial damage on Iran.
"Watch this space for more announcements coming next week because we are going to apply measures never seen in the history of economic isolation on a country," he said in an interview on Newsmax's 'Rob Schmitt Tonight’ programme.
Mr Trump is under pressure at home to end the unpopular war, with high fuel prices dragging down his approval ratings and potentially eroding his party's control of Congress in midterm elections in November.
Benchmark Brent futures and US West Texas Intermediate crude futures were both up slightly at about $87 (€75) and $81 (€70) a barrel respectively.
India's reliance on Russian crude surged to a record in July, while refineries in Asia, a major customer for fuel from the Gulf, bought US crude this week to ensure future supplies.
Iran has previously said it will not allow the waterway to reopen until its conditions are met.
These include removing economic sanctions and releasing frozen Iranian assets.
Yesterday, an Iranian parliamentary committee approved Iran's plan for the strait.
It includes a provision banning the transit of US, Israeli and other "hostile" countries' assets and equipment, the semi-official Tasnim news agency reported.
The US lifted its blockade of Iran's shipping and ports for a month in mid-June but has since reimposed it, cutting off Iran's primary source of hard currency and compounding earlier losses from wartime strikes on its energy infrastructure.
The United States previously said it would lift the Iranian blockade once Iran and Oman, which sit on either side of the strait, reach an agreement to restore commercial shipping.
Mr Trump has also repeatedly threatened to escalate military strikes and "hit Iran hard", although he has thus far resisted deploying ground troops or seizing strategic islands and bombing desalination plants.
Earlier this week, Mr Trump suggested he would rely on economic means, rather than military action.
The US has tightened economic sanctions against Iran and other individuals and entities that it said are helping it procure weapons, but the pressure campaign has not brought Iran back to the negotiating table.
Reports that Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis had targeted a Saudi Aramco refinery with drones yesterday renewed concerns about a widening regional war.
Global economists have forecast a sharp drop in global growth, and potentially a swing into recession in some areas, warning that the impact would grow if the war was not ended soon.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the U.S. Navy can sustain its blockade of Iranian ports for an unlimited period by rotating ships through the region as Washington continues military and economic pressure on Tehran.
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom
The United States has enough naval capacity to maintain its blockade of Iranian ports indefinitely, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Thursday, signaling that the Pentagon believes it can continue restricting Iranian shipping without placing a fixed time limit on the operation.
Hegseth said the Navy can sustain the blockade by rotating vessels into and out of the Middle East as deployments require.
“Indefinitely the United States Navy can maintain a blockade like that because we’ll rotate ships in and out, as we have, and we’ll continue to,” Hegseth told reporters.
His comments indicate that the military has advised President Donald Trump that the blockade can remain in place for as long as the administration considers it necessary while Washington seeks to increase pressure on Iran and revive negotiations aimed at ending the conflict.
Those negotiations have so far failed to produce an agreement.
The war began Feb. 28 with U.S.-Israeli strikes against Iran, and the United States has since significantly expanded its military presence across the Middle East.
Hegseth made his remarks in Panama after addressing sailors aboard the USS Gridley, a guided-missile destroyer that had previously deployed to the Middle East.
The defense secretary’s comments came one day after Trump declared that the United States had established control over the Strait of Hormuz, the strategically important waterway connecting the Persian Gulf with international shipping routes.
“The U.S.A. has total control over the Strait of Hormuz. I THINK WE WILL KEEP IT! Our Naval Blockade is being called, by everyone, ‘A WALL OF STEEL,’ and there is nothing Iran can do about it,” Trump wrote Wednesday on Truth Social.
The Strait of Hormuz has been a central focus of the conflict because of its importance to global energy markets.
Before the war, approximately one-fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas shipments moved through the strait.
Following the Feb. 28 attacks, Tehran effectively shut the waterway.
The United States subsequently established a naval blockade targeting Iranian shipping and Iranian ports while maintaining that commercial vessels traveling to and from non-Iranian ports would continue to receive protection for freedom of navigation.
Washington has committed tens of thousands of American troops to the Middle East since hostilities began.
More than 20 U.S. warships have also been deployed to the region as part of the military buildup.
The naval operation has increasingly involved direct enforcement against commercial vessels accused of attempting to bypass the blockade.
Since the blockade began, U.S. forces have redirected more than 55 commercial vessels attempting to run it, according to the information provided.
American forces have disabled three vessels and boarded two others during enforcement operations.
One of the most recent confrontations occurred earlier this week when a U.S. Navy MH-60 helicopter fired two Hellfire missiles into the engine room of a Panama-flagged vessel after the ship ignored warnings from U.S. forces, according to the military.
The episode demonstrated the level of force Washington is prepared to use to enforce restrictions on maritime traffic connected to Iran.
Hegseth’s statement Thursday also addresses questions about whether the Navy can sustain such an operation over a prolonged period.
Rather than keeping the same ships deployed indefinitely, the Pentagon intends to maintain the blockade by cycling vessels and crews through the theater.
That strategy would allow the United States to preserve its maritime pressure on Iran while eventually replacing ships that have spent extended periods in the region.
The blockade is intended to place additional economic pressure on Tehran while the Trump administration continues seeking a negotiated end to the war.
With diplomacy so far producing no agreement, Hegseth said the military does not face an immediate operational deadline that would force Washington to abandon the blockade.
Trump, meanwhile, has publicly presented American control of the Strait of Hormuz as a major strategic advantage and indicated Wednesday that the United States may seek to retain that position.
Together, the statements from Trump and Hegseth suggest that Washington is preparing for the possibility of a prolonged maritime campaign.
As long as negotiations remain unresolved, the administration appears prepared to continue using U.S. naval power to restrict Iranian ports and shipping while keeping non-Iranian commercial traffic moving through the region.
Hegseth’s declaration that the blockade can continue “indefinitely” makes clear that, from the Pentagon’s perspective, maintaining the operation is primarily a matter of rotating sufficient ships and personnel rather than reaching the limits of U.S. naval capacity.

sources.news_title: US Can Maintain Naval Blockade Of Iran "Indefinitely", Says Pete Hegseth
Hegseth says US can maintain Iran blockade ‘indefinitely’ as Strait of Hormuz standoff deepens
sources.text:
The United States has enough military assets to maintain its naval blockade of Iran indefinitely, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said on Thursday (August 13), signalling that Washington is prepared to sustain pressure on Tehran as efforts to end the conflict remain stalled.
Hegseth said the US Navy could keep ships in the region for as long as necessary by rotating vessels in and out of the area.
“Indefinitely the United States Navy can maintain a blockade like that because we'll rotate ships in and out, as we have, and we'll continue to,” Hegseth told reporters.
Hegseth made the comments in Panama after addressing the crew of the USS Gridley, a guided-missile destroyer that had previously deployed to the Middle East.
The US has deployed tens of thousands of troops to the Middle East since the war began, including more than 20 warships, according to the report.
Hegseth's comments came a day after Trump claimed that the United States had established control over the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial global energy route.
“The U.S.A. has total control over the Strait of Hormuz,” Trump wrote on Truth Social, describing the US naval blockade as a “WALL OF STEEL.”
The Strait had effectively been closed by Iran after the war began with US-Israeli strikes on February 28. Before the conflict, about one-fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas shipments passed through the waterway.
Since imposing the blockade, US forces have redirected more than 55 commercial vessels attempting to breach it, according to the report. Three ships have been disabled and two boarded.
Earlier this week, a US Navy MH-60 helicopter fired two Hellfire missiles into the engine room of a Panama-flagged vessel after the ship allegedly ignored warnings from US forces.
Washington has said its blockade is aimed at Iranian shipping and ports while maintaining freedom of navigation for vessels travelling to and from non-Iranian ports.
Despite months of US military strikes that have targeted Iran's leadership and damaged parts of its military capabilities, including its navy, Tehran has continued to exert influence over the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran has retaliated with missile and drone attacks against US allies in the region and has targeted commercial vessels travelling through the strait without its permission.
The continued confrontation has kept the strategically important waterway at the centre of the conflict and raised the prospect of prolonged disruption to global energy supplies.
Trump has repeatedly shifted between threats of further escalation and claims that a peace agreement could be close.
The president has so far resisted some of the most escalatory options, including deploying ground troops, seizing strategic islands and targeting desalination plants.
The administration faces pressure to bring the conflict to an end as the November midterm elections approach. High fuel prices have emerged as a major concern, particularly in rural areas that have traditionally supported Trump.
Hegseth has rejected reports of deteriorating conditions and declining morale aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, calling accounts of problems on the aircraft carrier “completely misrepresented.”
The 5,000-person carrier has been at sea since November 2025 and has been deployed to the Middle East since January, supporting US military operations in the war with Iran.
Hegseth defended the Navy’s efforts to support the crew, saying sailors on extended deployments were operating under difficult conditions.
“We make sure every ship, every crew, every captain has everything we can provide them at every single moment,” Hegseth told reporters during a visit to Panama.
The prolonged deployment of the Abraham Lincoln has raised concerns about the physical and mental strain on its crew. Sailors have remained on heightened alert amid the threat of drone and missile attacks from Iran.
Reports of suicide attempts and declining morale have added to concerns about the impact of the extended mission on sailors' mental health.
(With Reuters inputs)

U.S. says it can keep naval blockade on Iran ‘indefinitely,’ vows more economic pressure
PANAMA CITY – The United States on Thursday said that it could maintain a naval blockade of Iran indefinitely and would ratchet up economic pressure on Tehran as ceasefire talks have floundered, global oil supply is dropping and regional tensions are rising.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told reporters that the U.S. military has the capability to maintain a naval presence in the region to enforce its blockade of Iran, which has inflicted severe economic damage on the country.
“Indefinitely the United States Navy can maintain a blockade like that because we’ll rotate ships in and out, as we have, and we’ll continue to,” Hegseth told reporters during a trip to Panama.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Thursday that the United States planned to inflict more financial damage on Iran.
“Watch this space for more announcements coming next week because we are going to apply measures like have never been seen in the history of economic isolation on a country,” he said in an interview on Newsmax’s “Rob Schmitt Tonight” program.
With a tentative June deal to end the war in tatters, Iran has sought to exert leverage on Washington in return by controlling the Strait of Hormuz.
It has attacked some vessels trying to transit the strategic waterway, through which a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas traveled before the war began in February.
Two vessels from the state-owned Abu Dhabi National Oil Company were attacked transiting the strait Thursday evening, UAE state news agency WAM reported. The United Arab Emirates government condemned it as an Iranian attack.
U.S. President Donald Trump is under pressure at home to end a war that is deeply unpopular, with high fuel prices dragging down his approval ratings and potentially eroding his party’s control of Congress in November’s midterm elections .
Trump has repeatedly asserted that the U.S. has “total control” over the strait, prompting Iranian denials. Tehran has said it will not allow the waterway to reopen until its conditions are met. These include removing economic sanctions and releasing frozen Iranian assets.
Shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz fell to eight vessels on Tuesday, compared with a 10-day average of about 12 vessels, and 130 to 140 ships before the war.
The U.S. lifted its blockade of Iran’s shipping and ports for a month in mid-June but has since reimposed it, cutting off Tehran’s primary source of hard currency and compounding earlier losses from wartime strikes on its energy infrastructure.
Washington previously said it would lift the Iranian blockade once Iran and Oman, which sit on either side of the strait, reach an agreement to restore commercial shipping.
Shrinking oil supply
Trump has also repeatedly threatened to escalate military strikes and “hit Iran hard,” although he has thus far resisted deploying ground troops or seizing strategic islands and bombing desalination plants. Earlier this week, Trump suggested he would rely on economic means, rather than military action.
The U.S. has tightened economic sanctions against Iran and other individuals and entities that it says are helping it procure weapons, but the pressure campaign has failed to bring Tehran back to the negotiating table.
Stress is mounting on the global economy. The International Energy Agency on Wednesday forecast that global oil supply would fall by 4.3 million barrels per day, or around 4%, this year.
Just a month ago, the agency had forecast a drop of 3.7 million barrels per day.
Oil prices settled down more than 2% on Thursday after a week of gain, as investors focused on signs of weaker global demand and a sharp increase in U.S. crude inventories.
But reports that Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis had targeted a Saudi Aramco refinery with drones unsettled the market, renewing concerns about a widening regional war.
Economists have forecast a sharp drop in global growth as a result of the war, and potentially a swing into recession in some areas, warning that the impact will grow if the war is not ended soon.
Hegseth declined to comment on a question about whether, in retrospect, it was a mistake to declare a ceasefire in April, a move that ended high-tempo bombing of Iran in exchange for peace negotiations that have failed to resolve the conflict.
“I’m never going to comment on that. We’re doing exactly what we need to, to ensure that Iran never has a nuclear weapon,” Hegseth said.

sources.news_title: Volatility Exits Crypto And TradFi As U.S.-Iran Risks And Sovereign Debt Linger
sources.text:
The calm in crypto is no longer a crypto-only story. A day-ahead market brief from CoinDesk on Aug. 14 described volatility draining out of both digital assets and traditional finance, even while U.S.-Iran risks stay in place and sovereign debt keeps rising. That combination matters because it changes where the next repricing is likely to come from.
The Numbers Behind the Calm
That drain in volatility shows up clearest in the options market. Bitcoin’s 30-day implied volatility index, BVIV, has slipped back to a 2026 low near 36%, reversing a brief spike to nearly 38% earlier this week. Ether shows the same pattern. On Wall Street, the VIX — the S&P 500’s benchmark fear gauge — has fallen to its lowest level since January. Even the bond market’s equivalent, the MOVE index, is drifting toward the low end of its multi-month 66%-84% range, and volatility gauges for gold and oil are easing too.
That’s notable because the MOVE index tracks Treasury notes, which underpin pricing across global finance. When Treasury volatility rises, it tends to tighten financial conditions broadly and push risk assets lower together. Its decline now suggests bond traders aren’t pricing in near-term shocks, even as headline risk stays elevated: the U.S. has said its naval blockade of Iranian ports could continue “indefinitely,” and 10-year Treasury yields climbed to 4.661% Thursday on the back of that threat, with the 2-year at 4.152% and the 30-year at 5.237%.
Two Ways to Read the Same Chart
This is where the “next repricing” question splits into two camps. An efficient-markets view says the calm is simply markets correctly pricing all available information — nothing to see. A contrarian reading treats synchronized low volatility across crypto, equities, bonds, and commodities as exactly the setup that precedes a shock, since options are cheap to hedge against tail risk right when few investors think they need to.
Crypto’s Own Backdrop Hasn’t Been Calm
Bitcoin slipped below $63,000 this week as oil and yields climbed, and spot bitcoin ETFs logged their first two-day drawdown of August, a reversal from the steady inflow streaks funds had posted earlier in the month. Regulatory catalysts didn’t help: the SEC canceled its long-awaited “Regulation Crypto” rulemaking meeting Friday without setting a new date, and a separate “innovation exemption” for tokenization was pushed back again amid pushback from Wall Street and the White House — the latest in a run of delayed crypto rulemaking efforts this summer. XRP, meanwhile, has been hovering near the $1 level.
